headline: Hi, I'm *Vlad*.
tagline: From writing code to designing systems

paragraphs: 7 years, I've worked across fintech, social platforms, healthcare, and enterprise workforce management.

This isn't my CV. It's the story of the problems that changed how I think, in about 5 minutes. I want to show how I grew as an engineer — from learning the fundamentals of JavaScript and React, to owning critical modules, making architectural decisions, working with large-scale systems, and thinking about stability and users.

title: Capital Holding
subtitle: Frontend Developer · April 2019 — October 2020

paragraphs: My first position as a frontend developer, on a product used for live sports betting.
It was the first time I had to understand how a real application is built — not just how to write code, but how different pieces work together.

cards.description: My first real product: a betting platform where the numbers on screen changed every few seconds, and we built every part of it ourselves.
cards.detail: Building everything by hand meant I had to learn how the web actually works, not just how to use tools that hide it. That foundation made everything I learned afterwards make sense.

cards.description: The first project ended and a new betting platform began — this time built with React, the tool most modern websites are made with today.
cards.detail: Having built the hard way first, I could see exactly which problems these tools were invented to solve — so I learned why they work, not just how to use them.

transition: One year, two products, one team. I had no idea how narrow that was.

title: DataMix
tagline: The first time I understood that engineering is a team sport.
subtitle: Frontend Engineer · October 2020 — December 2021

paragraphs: My first outsourced experience. Instead of staying on one product, I worked across different projects, domains and requirements — and grew from junior to a strong mid-level engineer in just over a year.
It was also the first place where I experienced a genuinely warm engineering environment. That mattered more than I expected.

transition: Different domains, different constraints. Two projects taught me the most.

title: DataMix
tagline: The projects that taught me the most.

cards.title: Investment platform
cards.description: One of the main developers on a platform matching investors with companies looking for funding.
cards.detail: Heavy calculations and a lot of data moving at once. That's where I learned that making a product feel fast has less to do with the screen than with how you organise the information behind it.

cards.title: Social media platform
cards.description: The only frontend developer on an Instagram-style social network — from an empty folder to a working product in six months.
cards.detail: Design, animations, performance, releases — every decision was mine, and there was nobody to pass a problem to. It's the fastest I've ever learned.

blocks.heading: Engineering is more than writing code
items: It's reading someone else's work before it ships.
It's sitting with another engineer until the problem makes sense.
It's arguing about how something should be built — before anyone builds it.
It's remembering there's a person on the other end of every decision.
It's fixing something nobody asked you to fix.

transition: That's when I started seeing frontend engineering as a responsibility, not just a job.

title: REMED
tagline: Software that people's health depended on.
subtitle: Frontend Engineer · December 2021 — August 2024

paragraphs: A healthcare CRM connecting doctors, clinics, laboratories and healthcare workflows with external healthcare systems.
It integrated with Helsi (Ukraine's national eHealth system), and  contained some of the most heavily used modules I'd worked with up to that point.

badges.label: Connected to the country's health system

transition: Doctors used some of these screens every hour of every day. Those were the ones I owned.

title: REMED
subtitle: What I was responsible for

cards.title: The busiest screens in the clinic
cards.description: I owned the three most heavily used modules — the doctor's workplace, the cash desk and the scheduling calendar — screens doctors relied on every hour of the day.

cards.title: Modular architecture
cards.description: The code was arranged the way a clinic thinks — patients, visits, payments — so changing one area didn't ripple through the others.

cards.title: Mentoring
cards.description: Near-weekly deep dives on a technology the team picked, like Redux Saga or Tailwind, plus code reviews and pairing — half of what I know well, I know because I had to explain it.

cards.title: E2E testing
cards.description: Automated tests that clicked through booking a visit, the way a real user would — so a broken step was caught before a doctor hit it mid-appointment.

transition: Everything I'd learned about boundaries was about to be tested at a different scale.

title: WorkJam
tagline: The most complicated frontend environment I'd worked in.
subtitle: Senior Frontend Engineer · March 2024 — July 2026

paragraphs: Around 3 million people use it to get through their working day. A frontline workforce platform: scheduling, tasks, communication, learning, compliance, and integrations with whatever a company already runs.

Multiple applications. Shared packages. A large monorepo. Multiple teams. And an architecture that let new React features run inside the old Angular apps, so the product could move forward without being rebuilt.

blocks.heading: What the platform runs on
blocks.note: Two frameworks, several applications, one product.

blocks.text: The hard part wasn't building the new platform. It was living with both.

title: WorkJam · Case Study
eyebrow: Replacing a system the whole product depended on
tagline: How do you replace something everything relies on, without anyone noticing?

paragraphs: Feature flags are the switches that decide which parts of a product each company sees. Every one of our applications depended on them, through a single shared library at the centre of the platform.
Those switches ran on two outside services that had to go — while 3 million people used the product every day. I owned that migration.

steps.label: Proposed the move, then researched what it would really cost
Added the new system alongside the old two
Three flag systems running at once
Covered every affected page with automated tests
QA, then staging, then a handful of real companies
Watched production for a month, then removed the old systems

blocks.text: Three flag systems became one. Zero downtime, no incidents, no rollbacks — and nobody outside the team noticed.

title: WorkJam · Case Study

cards.title: Proposed a better plan
cards.description: Worked with the product owner and suggested reusing the calendar we already had, instead of building a second one beside it.

cards.title: Left the code better than I found it
cards.description: Refactored the existing calendar so both views could be built from the same pieces — cleaner and reusable, not just finished.

cards.title: Delivered five days early
cards.description: Ten days instead of the fifteen planned, with the harder parts done first.

cards.title: Shipped without a bug
cards.description: Covered end to end with automated tests — nothing came back from QA or from production.

paragraphs: A product owner wanted to bundle two epics: a brand-new date picker and a calendar view built on top of it. I estimated the new picker at about 10 days and showed the numbers.
Instead, I proposed extending the existing date picker to match the new design. It shipped in 3 days instead of 10, and the client was happy with the result.

blocks.text: The important part wasn't writing code faster — it was solving the right problem.

tagline: Twice, the smaller plan was the better plan.

paragraphs: The platform consisted of four module applications and one unified application, and we needed to integrate them with Microsoft Teams.
Five applications had to behave like one product inside Microsoft Teams: four module apps, and the unified app that ties them together.

I built one shared place that holds everything Teams needs — the configuration, who the user is, which company they belong to — so every application reads it the same way instead of each team solving it again. Clean in one place, rather than copied five times.

The hardest part was moving between apps. Inside Teams, clicking a link couldn't just change the page — it had to open a different app while keeping who the user is and where they were. I built navigation between the apps that carries that context across.

blocks.text: Solve the integration once. Make every application benefit from it.

title: WorkJam · Case Study
eyebrow: Web Chat Inside the Android App
tagline: One chat, two platforms, no second login.

paragraphs: The Android app needed the platform's web chat, but Google's new 4KB page size requirement meant the chat module couldn't be loaded into the app directly.
I rendered it inside a WebView to keep the native app light, and built a bridge so the web chat and the Android app could talk to each other.

cards.title: Already signed in
cards.description: People logged into the app are logged into the chat automatically, with no second login screen.

cards.title: Native features from the web
cards.description: The web chat can open the phone's camera, record video and take screenshots through the bridge.

blocks.text: Keep the native app light, and let the web do what it already does well.

title: WorkJam · Case Study
eyebrow: AI in the Product and in the Workflow
tagline: Help people write, right where they write.

paragraphs: The rich text editor is one shared component behind documents, posts and comments across the platform. Writing good content in it takes time, so I added an AI assistant (built on Gemini) directly inside it — the way Jira helps you write a task.
The model sees the full post. People pick a quick action or describe exactly what they need in their own words.

cards.title: Faster writing
cards.description: A rough draft becomes a polished post in seconds, without leaving the editor.

cards.title: One place, everywhere
cards.description: The editor is shared, so documents, posts and comments all get the assistant at once.

cards.title: Answers appear as they're written
cards.description: The text streams in and shows up immediately, so nobody waits on a blank screen.

cards.title: Ready to use
cards.description: The output arrives already styled, so there's nothing to reformat.

blocks.heading: And AI for the team: translations in 50+ languages

steps.label: Before: spreadsheet, script, PR, review, version bump — about 5 hours
Developer writes the new keys in one JSON file
One AI command generates all 50+ languages
It opens the pull request with the ticket link and description

blocks.text: AI where people write, and AI where engineers work — both built once, used everywhere.

title: How I Think About Engineering
tagline: The technology changed. The way I think changed more.
subtitle: What 7+ years of frontend engineering taught me

items: Shipping end to end taught me what production actually costs.
Frameworks taught me how to structure interfaces.
Working across projects taught me how to collaborate.
Ownership taught me to think beyond individual features.
Large-scale systems taught me about boundaries, migration and reliability.

items.title: Boundaries
items.description: Split by domain, own the module.

transition: What I thought about changed as the systems got bigger. A few things didn't.

title: Principles
tagline: The things that survived every stack I worked in.
subtitle: Six ideas I keep coming back to

cards.title: Clear boundaries
cards.description: Complex systems become easier to change when responsibilities are clearly separated.

cards.title: Simple code
cards.description: Enterprise software doesn't have to mean complicated software.

cards.title: Ownership
cards.description: If you own a module, you should understand its users, constraints, dependencies and failure modes.

cards.title: Pragmatism
cards.description: The newest technology isn't always the answer. Sometimes improving what exists is the better decision.

cards.title: Stability
cards.description: A production system is not a playground. Every change has users behind it.

cards.title: Collaboration
cards.description: Good engineering decisions rarely happen in isolation.

tagline: Technologies I've worked with in production
subtitle: Tools are means, not the destination.
transition: But a stack doesn't tell you how someone thinks. The problems they choose to solve do.

title: What's Next?
tagline: Got a frontend that's hard to change? That's my favourite kind of problem.
subtitle: Remote or hybrid · Wrocław, Poland

paragraphs: I do my best work when I own an area end to end: its users, its architecture, its failure modes — influencing architectural decisions and working alongside talented engineers.
I believe enterprise platforms can be written with clear and simple code. The key is setting clear boundaries and responsibilities between modules.
This site has its own AI assistant, built with Node.js and the Claude SDK, that answers questions about my experience — tested by a second AI that plays the recruiter and checks the answers.

cards.title: Technical challenges
cards.description: High-load modules, performance problems and systems that require real technical thinking.

cards.title: Ownership
cards.description: Clear responsibilities and the ability to own a module or area end to end.

cards.title: Growth
cards.description: Deepening my frontend expertise while moving toward broader full-stack responsibilities.

cards.title: People & culture
cards.description: A warm, supportive team and a manager who listens and genuinely cares about development.

blocks.text: Maybe the next chapter is something we build together.
